issues.legal_issue: A land-acquisition notice issued before an amendment lapses when the declaration is made after the mandatory transition period prescribed for pending acquisitions.
material_facts: The preliminary acquisition notification and notice to interested persons were issued on 1 May 1980, before the 1981 Amendment Act came into force on 27 June 1981.
The declaration of acquisition was made on 19 March 1987, more than two years after the amendment commenced.
The amendment prescribed a two-year limit for declarations concerning notices issued before its commencement; its separate three-year limit applied to notices issued after commencement.
issues.conclusion: The preliminary notification had lapsed because the declaration was made after the mandatory two-year transition period, and the later declaration was legally unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(2) of the 1981 Amendment Act, beginning with a non obstante clause and using the words “no declaration” and “shall be made,” imposed a mandatory, non-departable two-year limit for declarations concerning pre-amendment notices. The three-year proviso inserted into Section 6 of the 1953 Act applied to post-amendment notices. Section 5(1)(b) did not displace the specific limit in Section 5(2). The Court distinguished Indrapuri Grah Nirman Sahakari Samiti Ltd. and Chain Singh because they did not govern this statutory scheme, and held Pesara Pushapmala Reddy irrelevant.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and notice_before_amendment and amendment_transition_limit and declaration_after_transition_deadline

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated a proceeding to acquire land compulsorily.
predicates.notice_before_amendment: The government issued the preliminary acquisition notice before an amendment governing pending acquisitions came into force.
predicates.amendment_transition_limit: The amendment prescribed a mandatory deadline for declarations in acquisitions initiated before it came into force.
predicates.declaration_after_transition_deadline: The government made the acquisition declaration after the deadline applicable to the earlier notice had expired.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition proceeding involves a notice issued before an amendment that sets a mandatory transition deadline, a declaration made after that deadline means the preliminary notice has lapsed.

issues.legal_issue: The government cannot dispense with the landowner's objection inquiry on urgency grounds without genuine immediate urgency, particularly after prolonged inaction and without supporting material.
material_facts: The preliminary notification stated that the land was needed for construction of a bus stand, but the government invoked urgency and dispensed with the inquiry only when it made the declaration nearly seven years later.

During that interval, the government took no steps to commence the objection inquiry, although the inquiry could have been completed in a few months and few owners or interested persons were involved.
The government's explanation asserted that urgency was apparent from the public purpose but supplied no material showing that delay for the inquiry would defeat that purpose.
Construction of the proposed bus stand would itself take time.
issues.conclusion: The exercise of urgency powers and dispensation of the objection inquiry were legally unsustainable because real urgency was not established and the landowners' valuable right to object was taken away without justification.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5-A and 17(1) and (4) of the 1953 Act, read consistently with Article 300-A, require the lawful procedure for compulsory acquisition to be followed. The right to object under Section 5-A is substantial and valuable; dispensing with it is an exceptional power justified only where genuine urgency cannot brook the delay of even a few weeks or months. The government must apply its mind and, when challenged, provide material supporting the urgency; pre- and post-notification delay is relevant, particularly where no such material is produced. The Court relied on Nandeshwar Prasad v. U.P. Govt., Munshi Singh v. Union of India, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, Anand Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Radhy Shyam v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and urgency_power_invoked and objection_inquiry_dispensed and prolonged_inaction and no_inquiry_steps and no_urgency_material and purpose_allows_inquiry_delay

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated a proceeding to acquire land compulsorily.
predicates.urgency_power_invoked: The government invoked its special power on the ground that the acquisition was urgent.
predicates.objection_inquiry_dispensed: The government dispensed with the inquiry that would allow interested persons to object to the acquisition.
predicates.prolonged_inaction: A substantial interval passed after the preliminary notice before the government invoked urgency.
predicates.no_inquiry_steps: The government took no steps during that interval to commence the objection inquiry.
predicates.no_urgency_material: The government produced no material showing that conducting the inquiry would defeat the public purpose.
predicates.purpose_allows_inquiry_delay: The nature of the proposed public project allowed time for the objection inquiry to be conducted.

issues.definition: When the government invokes urgency to dispense with an objection inquiry after prolonged inaction, takes no steps to conduct the inquiry, produces no supporting urgency material, and pursues a project that allows time for inquiry, the dispensation is invalid.
